# Solutions to the arguments.
</margin>

The answer to the first argument is clear: there is no doubt that, just as men can kill by God’s permission, so can they truly and really remove that member or others. But in such cases, demons do not operate through the witches of whom mention is now made. Through this, the solution to the second argument is also clear. However, regarding the point that because God further permits the <term>vim generatiuam</term> <gloss>generative power</gloss> to be bewitched for certain reasons, He therefore also permits that member to be truly and really removed—this is not valid as a general rule. This is because it would not be done by way of a <term>maleficii</term> <gloss>spell or curse</gloss>, nor do witches desire this when they perform such works; they prefer not to lose the power of restoring the member when they wish and know how. From this, it is clear that it is removed not truly, but by a <term>prestigiosa arte</term> <gloss>deceptive or illusory art</gloss>. To the third argument regarding the transformation of <term>vxoris loth</term> <gloss>Lot’s wife</gloss>, we say: that was a true transformation and not by illusory art; however, we are now speaking of illusory art. To the fourth, that demons can induce certain substantial forms and therefore also remove them: it is said regarding the <term>magos pharaonis</term> <gloss>magicians of Pharaoh</gloss> that they made true serpents; and demons can produce certain effects concerning some imperfect creatures with the aid of some other agent, which they cannot do regarding humans, for whom God has greater care. According to the scripture: "Does God have care for oxen?" <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 9:9</note>. They can, however, always—as has been said—harm humans truly and really or even by illusory art, provided God permits it. Through this, the solution to the last argument is also clear.

<margin>
# Question 10. Whether witches work upon men by transforming them into bestial forms through illusory art.
</margin>

Fourthly, the truth itself is declared where humans are also transformed into beasts. Regarding how this may happen, it is argued that it is not possible for this to occur. In the twenty-sixth <term>quaestio</term>, fifth <term>episcopi</term>, from the Council of Ancyra: "Whoever believes that any creature can be changed either for the better or for the worse, or transformed into another species or another likeness, except by the Creator Himself who made all things and through whom all things were made, is undoubtedly an infidel and worse than a pagan." Let us also use the arguments of <term>sancti Thome</term> <gloss>Saint Thomas Aquinas</gloss> in the second book of the Sentences, distinction eight, on whether demons can impress themselves upon the <term>sensus corporales</term> <gloss>bodily senses</gloss> by deluding them with illusions. Where first he argues that they cannot. For that form of a beast which is seen must be somewhere; but it cannot be only in the sense, because the sense does not have any <term>speciem</term> <gloss>mental image or appearance</gloss> except that which is received from things. And there is no true beast present, according to the cited authority of the Canon. Nor, again, can it be in the thing that is seen—such as a woman appearing to be a beast—because two substantial forms cannot be in the same thing at one and the same time. Therefore, since that form of a beast which is seen can be nowhere, no <term>illusio prestigiosa</term> <gloss>deceptive illusion</gloss> can occur in the eye of the beholder, since vision must necessarily be terminated by some form. Furthermore, if it is said that the form is in the surrounding air, this cannot be: first, because air is not receptive to any form or figure; and second, because the same air cannot always remain around that person due to its fluidity, especially when the person moves; and thirdly, because such a transformation would then be seen by everyone, which does not happen, since demons are not seen to deceive at least the visions of holy men. Furthermore, the visual sense or visual power is a passive power. But every passive thing is moved by an active thing proportioned to it. The active thing proportioned to the sense is twofold: one as if originating the act, namely the object; the other as if carrying it, such as the medium. But that form which is seen cannot be the object of the sense nor even the medium carrying it. Regarding the first—that it cannot be the object—this is because it cannot be taken from any real thing, as touched upon in the preceding argument, since it is not in the sense as something accepted from a thing, nor in the thing itself, nor even in the air itself as if in a carrying medium, as was touched upon in the third argument. Furthermore, if a demon moves the internal cognitive power, he does this either by presenting himself...

<summary>This page addresses the theological debate over whether physical transformations or disappearances caused by witches are real or illusory. It cites Saint Thomas Aquinas to argue that most bestial transformations are deceptive illusions affecting human perception rather than changes in physical substance.</summary>
<keywords>illusory art, substantial form, Lot's wife, magicians of Pharaoh, Saint Thomas Aquinas, Council of Ancyra, sensory perception, demonic deception, lycanthropy, canon law</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>God, and they command that he be worshiped everywhere. But people of an unlearned and impious nature—to whom fate has truly not granted the ability to obtain gifts from the gods, nor to possess knowledge of the immortal Jove <note>original: "Iouis"; Jupiter, often identified in this context with the supreme divine principle</note>—not listening to either the gods or to divine men, have rejected all the gods. Instead of following the prohibition against demons, they have chosen not only to not pursue them with hatred, but even to revere them. While pretending to worship God, they do not perform those acts through which alone God is adored. For God, being the father of all, needs nothing; but it is well with us when we adore him through justice, chastity, and other virtues, making our very life a prayer to him through imitation and inquiry concerning him. For inquiry purifies, he says, and imitation deifies the affection by working toward him. He indeed preached well about God the father and spoke of the manners in which he should be worshiped. The prophetic books of the Hebrews are full of these precepts, when the life of the saints is either praised or blamed.

But regarding the Christians, he either says as much or calumniates as much as the demons—whom he considers gods—desire. As if it were difficult for anyone to recall what shameful and disgraceful things were performed in the service of the gods in theaters and temples, and to attend to what is read, said, and heard in the churches, or what is offered to the true God; and from this to understand where the building up and where the ruin of morals lies. Who told or inspired this man with such a vain and open lie: that the Christians revere the demons who were prohibited from being worshiped by the Hebrews, rather than hating them? But that God whom the wise men of the Hebrews worshiped forbids sacrifice even to the holy celestial angels and the powers of God—whom we, in this mortal pilgrimage of ours, venerate and love as most blessed fellow citizens—thundering in his law which he gave to his Hebrew people, and very threateningly brought forth, saying: He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out.

And lest anyone should think it was commanded that sacrifice not be made only to the most wicked demons and earthly spirits—whom this man calls the least or lesser—because in the holy scriptures they themselves are called gods, not those of the Hebrews

<column-break/>

but of the nations: which the seventy translators <note>The Septuagint: the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> evidently placed in the Psalm, saying: For all the gods of the nations are demons. Therefore, lest anyone should think it was prohibited to sacrifice to these demons, but permitted to sacrifice to the celestial ones, either all or some of them, he immediately added: except to the Lord alone; that is, except to the Lord only. This was so that no one might believe the phrase "to the Lord alone" refers to the Sun-god <note>original: "deum solem"; a pun on "soli" (alone) and "Soli" (to the Sun)</note> to whom he thinks sacrifice should be made. That it is not to be understood this way is very easily found in the Greek scriptures.

Therefore, the God of the Hebrews, to whom even this great philosopher bears such great testimony, gave the law to his Hebrew people. It was written in the Hebrew language, not obscure and unknown, but now spread abroad among all nations. In this law it is written: He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out, except to the Lord only. What need is there to search for many things regarding this matter in his law and his prophets? Rather, there is no need to search; for these things are not hidden or rare. One may collect things that are open and frequent, and place them in this disputation of mine, by which it appears clearer than light that the true and highest God wished sacrifice to be made to no one at all except himself. Behold this one thing said briefly, or rather grandly, threateningly, but truly, by that God whom the most learned of their men preach so excellently: let it be heard, let it be feared, let it be fulfilled, lest the rooting out of the disobedient follows.

He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out, he says, except to the Lord only. Not because he has need of anything, but because it is profitable for us that we should be his. For to him it is sung in the holy writings of the Hebrews: I have said to the Lord, you are my God, because you do not need my goods. Moreover, the most excellent and best sacrifice to him is ourselves. This is his city, the mystery of which we celebrate with our oblations, which are known to the faithful, as we have discussed in the preceding books. For the Hebrew prophets gave oracles that the victims which the Jews offered in the shadow of the future would cease, and that the nations from the rising of the sun to its setting would offer one sacrifice, just as we now see being done.

<summary>Augustine refutes Porphyry's claim that Christians worship demons, asserting that the God of the Hebrews strictly forbids sacrifice to any being but himself. He identifies the "true sacrifice" as the Christian community and its life of virtue, fulfilling Hebrew prophecies about the end of Jewish animal sacrifices.</summary>
<keywords>Porphyry, Demons, Sacrifice, Hebrew Law, Septuagint, Sun worship, City of God, Virtue, Liturgy</keywords>

Cherish me in your pious bosom alone, so that I may not feel the loss of life, let alone the loss of fame."

*Sorrow.* I am torn apart everywhere in the crossroads by the common folk.

*Reason.* Take it in good part. The common folk will make you known, virtue will make you famous, and conscience will make you secure.

---

### On the shame sought from unworthy praises.
## DIALOGUE XXVI.

> Praise sparingly, for when you praise unjustly,
> If you later condemn, it will be a sign of fickleness.

*Sorrow.* I am accused of having praised an unworthy man.

<note>A large ornamental initial L marks the start of the response from Reason.</note>

*Reason.* An evil thing is often born from a good root. For the good and innocent imagine others to be just as they are themselves. From this, they are even more prone to praise than is fair. And although I admit it is an evil thing to praise the unworthy, to disparage the undeserving is much worse.

*Sorrow.* I have praised an unworthy man.

*Reason.* If you did so knowingly, you are reprehensible; but if unknowingly, you are excusable. It is a lesser evil to be deceived than to deceive. To be deceived is someone else's fault; to deceive is the specific crime of the deceiver.

*Sorrow.* The praise of another turns to my infamy.

*Reason.* On the contrary, it is either your fault or your ignorance. From another person, just as there is no praise, so there is no infamy.

*Sorrow.* I grieve deeply that I praised an unworthy man.

*Reason.* See to it, then, that you do not grieve for this same thing often. Beware of leaping forward rashly to praise or to disparage. For there is a lust for both things and, to speak properly, a certain disease and itch of a moving tongue that knows no rest. The restraint and guarding of the tongue are numbered among the works of exceptional perfection, as the Scripture says:

<summary>Reason advises Sorrow on handling a damaged reputation and the error of praising unworthy individuals, noting that being deceived is better than deceiving others. The dialogue warns against the impulsive urge to praise or criticize, characterizing it as a lack of self-control.</summary>
<keywords>reputation, virtue, conscience, praise, gossip, integrity, self-restraint</keywords>

raw wool is applied. Olympias of Thebes <note>a famous midwife and medical writer of the 4th century BCE</note> added hyssop and nitre. The ash of a deer’s horn is drunk for the same purpose, as well as for a laboring <term>vulva</term> <gloss>womb</gloss>. Bull bile applied with two <term>oboli</term> <gloss>small weights</gloss> of opium is also an ointment. It is beneficial to fumigate the womb with deer hair. They report that female deer, when they sense they are pregnant, swallow a small stone, which is found in their excrement or in the womb (for it is found there too); this is kept tied as an amulet to preserve the pregnancy. Little bones are also found in the heart and womb which are very useful for pregnant women and those in labor. As for the pumice stone found in a similar way in the wombs of cows, we have spoken of it in the section on the nature of oxen. Wolf fat applied softens the womb. Their liver relieves its pains. Eating wolf meat is beneficial for those about to give birth, or if a wolf should be nearby when labor begins, it is so effective that it even acts as a defense against harmful applications. However, for a wolf to come upon a woman <note>unexpectedly</note> is said to be fatal.

There is also great use of the hare for women. The dried lung, when drunk, aids the womb. Its liver, drunk in water with Samian earth, stops excessive discharges. The <term>rennet</term> <gloss>stomach curd</gloss> aids the afterbirth. They should avoid baths from the previous day. Also, applied with saffron and leek juice on a tuft of wool, it expels dead fetuses. If the wombs of hares are taken in food, it is believed they conceive males. This is also achieved with their testicles and rennet. A hare fetus removed from the womb is said to bring back fertility to those who have ceased to bear children. But even for conception, the hare is healthy, and is given more frequently to the husband. Likewise, nine grains of its dung are given to a virgin so that her breasts may remain firm forever. This is also done with the rennet. For this reason, they smear blood with honey where they do not want plucked hairs to grow back. For swelling of the womb, it is useful to apply wild boar or swine dung with oil. The meal of dried dung is more effective at stopping it, or sprinkled into a drink if pregnant or newly delivered women are in pain.

Sow’s milk drunk with <term>mulsum</term> <gloss>honeyed wine</gloss> aids the delivery of women. Drunk by itself, it refills the failing breasts of nursing mothers. If the breasts of a young girl are smeared with sow’s blood, they grow less. If they are painful, they are soothed by drinking donkey milk. This, taken with added honey, also aids their purgations. The seasoned fat of the same animal heals ulcerations of the womb, and applied on wool, it softens any hardness of the womb. Used by itself, whether fresh or seasoned and applied with water, it has the power of a <term>psilothrum</term> <gloss>hair remover</gloss>. The seasoned spleen of the same animal applied with water causes an abundance of milk in the breasts. It corrects the womb when used as a fumigant. The hooves of a donkey, when used as a fumigant, ripen the birth so that it even calls forth an abortion; it is not used otherwise, as it kills a living fetus. If the fresh dung of the same animal is applied, it is said to wonderfully calm discharges of blood. Likewise the ash of the same dung, which also benefits the womb when applied. Hair is prevented from growing back if horse foam is applied for forty days before birth. The same is done with a decoction of deer horn; it is better if the horns are fresh. Horse milk is helpful for washing out the womb. If a dead fetus is suspected, the spleen drunk in sweet water ejects it. Likewise the fumigation of the hoof or dried dung.

Infused butter stops a prolapsed womb. An indurated womb is opened by bull bile mixed with oil of roses, with a tuft of wool and turpentine resin applied externally. They also say that a fumigation of dung from a male ox restrains a prolapsed womb and aids delivery. Conception is aided by drinking cow’s milk. It is certain that sterility can be caused by the distress of childbirth. Olympias of Thebes affirms this can be corrected by bull bile, snake fat, and verdigris with added honey, applied to the parts before intercourse. Calf bile, if used during purgations or sprinkled on the womb during intercourse, both softens the hardness of the belly and diminishes discharge at the navel, and generally benefits the womb. They set the measure of bile at one <term>denarius</term> <gloss>weight of a silver coin</gloss> mixed with a third part of celery and almond oil, as much as seems sufficient; this they apply on wool. The bile of a male calf ground with half as much honey is preserved for the womb. If they eat calf meat roasted with <term>aristolochia</term> <gloss>birthwort</gloss> around the time of conception, they are promised to give birth to males. Calf marrow boiled in wine and water with tallow is good for ulcerations of the womb. Likewise fox fat, and the excrement of cats applied with resin and rose oil. They think it most useful to fumigate the womb with goat horn. The blood of wild goats with sea-palm <note>possibly a type of seaweed or coral</note> removes hair. The bile of other goats, when sprinkled, softens callouses of the womb and facilitates conception after purgation. It also acts as a <term>psilothrum</term> <gloss>depilatory</gloss> if applied for three days after hairs are plucked. Midwives promise that any discharge, however immense, is stopped by drinking goat urine or if dung is applied. The membrane of goats, seasoned and taken in wine after the birth is delivered, expels the afterbirth. They think it useful to fumigate the womb with the hair of kids. And in a discharge of blood, the rennet is drunk or applied with henbane seed. Aeschines <note>an ancient writer on medicine or magic</note> says that if the loins of a woman are smeared with the blood of a wild black ox, a loathing for sex is produced. He also says the urine of a goat drunk with nard causes love, despite its offensiveness.

Nothing is more useful for infants than butter, by itself or with honey; specifically for teething, for the gums, and for mouth ulcers. A wolf’s tooth tied on as an amulet prevents the terrors of infants and diseases while teething. A wolf skin provides the same. Their largest teeth, tied to horses, are said to provide an untiring gait. An infant's diarrhea is stopped by rubbing the breast with hare rennet. Donkey liver with a small amount of <term>panace</term> <gloss>all-heal herb</gloss> dripped into the mouth protects infants from the falling sickness <note>epilepsy</note> and other diseases. They prescribe this for forty days. A donkey skin thrown over them makes infants fearless. The teeth that horses lose first, when tied on as amulets, provide easy teething for infants, more effectively if they have not touched the ground. Ox spleen is eaten in honey or applied for pains of the spleen. For running ulcers, it is used with honey. Calf spleen boiled in wine, crushed, and applied, heals small ulcers of the mouth. The brain of a goat passed through a gold ring and dripped into the mouths of infants before they are given milk protects against the falling sickness and other infant diseases. Goat dung tied in a cloth restrains restless infants, especially girls. Gums smeared with goat milk or hare brain make teething easy. Cato thinks that sleep is induced by eating hare. The common people also think it brings beauty to the body for nine days—a frivolous claim, yet there must be some underlying reason for such a strong belief. The Magi say that sleep is induced by the bile of a sacrificed goat, provided it is smeared on the eyes or placed under the pillow. The ash of goat horn with myrtle oil stops sweats when rubbed on. Sexual intercourse is stimulated by applying wild boar bile, or by a draught of pig marrow. Likewise, donkey fat mixed with the fat of a male goose. Also, according to Virgil, from the mating of a horse

<meta>continues from previous page: and the nature</meta> of their paths and circles is so positioned that they blow upon those watching at a certain time. Thus, although ships go with full sails, they nevertheless seem to stand still. Someone will eventually demonstrate in which parts <term>comets</term> <gloss>hairy stars</gloss> wander; why they travel so far removed from the others; how great and of what kind they are. We are content with what has been discovered; let posterity also contribute something to the truth. 

One says: "We do not see beyond the stars, but we transmit our gaze through comets." First, if that happens, it does not happen in that part where the star itself consists of thick and solid fire, but where a rare splendor runs out and is dispersed into hair. You see through the intervals between the fires, not through the fires themselves. He says: "All stars are round; comets are elongated, from which it appears they are not stars." For who will grant you that comets are long, when their nature indeed, like the others, is a globe? However, the brightness is extended just as the sun sends out its rays far and wide. Yet the form of the sun is one thing, and the form of the light that flows from it is another. Thus the body itself of comets is rounded, but the splendor appears longer than that of the other stars. 

"Why?" you ask. Tell me first: why does the moon receive a light so unlike the sun's, since it receives it from the sun? Why is it sometimes red, sometimes pale? Why does it have a livid and black color when it is excluded from the sight of the sun? Tell me why all the stars have faces somewhat unlike each other, and most different from the sun. Just as nothing prevents them from being stars even though they are not similar, so nothing prevents comets from being eternal and of the same lot as the rest, even if they do not have a similar face. 

Furthermore, if you consider this world itself, is it not composed of diverse things? Why is it that the sun always burns in the <term>Lion</term> <gloss>Leo</gloss> and scorches the earth with heat, yet in <term>the Water-bearer</term> <gloss>Aquarius</gloss> it binds the winter and closes the rivers with ice? And yet both this star and that are of the same condition <margin>† it rises</margin> even though they are dissimilar in effect and nature. Within a very short time the <term>Ram</term> <gloss>Aries</gloss> † is passed through <note>likely a corruption of "exoritur", rises</note>, the <term>Balance</term> <gloss>Libra</gloss> sinks most slowly, and yet both this star and that are of the same nature, though the former ascends in a brief time and the latter is drawn out for a long time. Do you not see how contrary the elements are among themselves? There are heavy and light, cold and hot, moist and dry. The entire concord of this world consists of discord. 

You deny that a comet is a star because its form does not correspond to the pattern, nor is it similar to the others. For you see, that star which returns to its place in the thirtieth year <note>Saturn</note> is very similar to this one which revisits its seat within a year. Nature does not perform her work according to a single form, but boasts in her very variety. She made some things more sluggish, others swifter than others. Some she made more powerful, others more temperate; some she led out from the crowd so that they might proceed as individuals and be conspicuous; some she sent into a flock. He is ignorant of the power of nature who does not think she is permitted at times to do anything except what she does more often. 

She does not show comets frequently; she assigned to them a different place, different times, and motions unlike the rest. She wished to honor the greatness of her work through these, whose face is more beautiful than you might think accidental, whether you consider their size or their brightness, which is greater and more fiery than the others. Indeed, the face has something notable and singular about it, not cast into a narrow space and cramped, but let down more freely, embracing the region of many stars. 

Aristotle says that comets signify storms and the intemperance of winds and rains. What then? Do you not judge that to be a star which announces future things? For it is not a sign of a storm in the same way that oil sparking and the growth of rotten fungi are signs of future rain; or in the way it is an indication of a raging sea if the coots play on dry land and desert the familiar marshes, and the heron flies above a high cloud. But it is so in the way the equinox signifies the turning of the year toward heat or cold; or how those things which the <term>Chaldaeans</term> <gloss>astrologers</gloss> chant signify what a star ordains as sad or joyful for those being born. 

So you may know this is so, a comet having risen does not immediately threaten winds and rains, as Aristotle says, but <margin>The rising of a comet makes the whole year suspect.</margin> it makes the entire year suspect. From which it appears that it did not draw signs from the immediate vicinity to give for the immediate future, but has them stored and compressed by the laws of the world. That comet which appeared in the consulship of Patriculus and Vopiscus <note>60 AD</note> brought about those things which were predicted by Aristotle and Theophrastus. For there were great and continuous storms everywhere; and in Achaia and Macedonia, cities were overthrown by earthquakes. 

"Their slowness," he says, "is an argument that they are heavier and have much of the earthy in them. Furthermore, their very courses are generally driven toward the poles." Both are false. I will speak of the former first: that things which are carried more slowly are heavy. What then? Is the star of Saturn, which performs its journey most slowly of all, heavy? And yet it has an argument for its lightness, because it is above the others. But you say it circles in a greater circuit,

<summary>Seneca refutes arguments that comets are not stars based on their shape or speed, emphasizing nature's variety and the long-term prophetic significance of cometary appearances.</summary>
<keywords>comets, Aristotle, Saturn, nature of stars, celestial mechanics, meteorology, Roman consuls</keywords>

but seized entire provinces and regions in a single stroke of calamity. And so, with foreign nations harassed and ruined, we saw Marseilles <note>original: "Massiliam"</note> carried in a triumphal procession as an example of our lost empire. A triumph was celebrated over that very city without whose help our generals never triumphed in wars beyond the Alps. I could recount many other wicked acts against our allies if the sun had ever looked upon anything more unworthy than this one alone. We are, therefore, justly punished. For unless we had endured their crimes without punishment, such great license never would have reached a single man. From him, indeed, the inheritance of private property came to a few, and the inheritance of wicked desires came to many. Indeed, the seed and cause of civil wars will never be lacking as long as ruined men both remember and hope for that bloody spear <note>the spear used to mark the auction of confiscated property</note>. Since Lucius Sulla had brandished it when his kinsman was dictator <note>referring to the auctions under the dictatorship of Sulla</note>, thirty-six years later it was taken up by one even more wicked <note>Julius Caesar</note>, and he did not shrink from that same spear. Another man, who had been a clerk during that earlier dictatorship, served as the city's financial official <term>quaestor urbanus</term> <gloss>a magistrate in charge of the state treasury and records</gloss> in this later one. From this it must be understood that as long as such rewards are offered, civil wars will never be lacking. And so, only the walls of the city now stand and remain, and even these are already fearing the ultimate crimes. But the Republic itself we have lost entirely. We have fallen into these disasters (to return to the main point) because we preferred to be feared rather than to be dear and loved. If such things could happen to the Roman people for ruling unjustly, what should individuals think?

The third article: whether more universal things are prior in our intellectual knowledge.

Regarding the third point, we proceed as follows. It seems that more universal things are not prior in our intellectual knowledge. First, because those things which are prior and better known according to nature are posterior and less known according to us. But universals are prior according to nature, because that from which the sequence of being does not return <note>original: "a quo non conuertitur subsistendi consequentia"</note> is prior; therefore, universals are posterior in the knowledge of our intellect. Furthermore, composite things are prior as far as we are concerned than simple things. But universals are simpler; therefore, they are known later by us. Furthermore, the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in the first book of the Physics that the thing defined comes into our knowledge before the parts of the definition. But more universal things are the parts of the definition of less universal things—just as "animal" is part of the definition of "man"—therefore, universals are known later by us. Furthermore, we arrive at causes and principles through effects. But universals are certain principles. Therefore, universals are known later by us. On the contrary is what is said in the first book of the Physics: that it is necessary to proceed from universals to singulars.

I respond that it must be said that in the knowledge of our intellect, two things must be considered. First, that intellectual knowledge in some way takes its beginning from sensitive knowledge. And because the sense is of singulars while the intellect is of universals, it is necessary that the knowledge of singulars is prior for us than the knowledge of universals. Second, it must be considered that our intellect proceeds from potentiality to act. Everything that proceeds from potentiality to act reaches an incomplete act—which is midway between potentiality and act—before reaching a perfect act. Now, the perfect act to which the intellect reaches is complete knowledge, through which things are known distinctly and determinately; however, the incomplete act is imperfect knowledge, through which things are known indistinctly under a certain confusion. For what is known in this way is known in a certain respect in act and in a certain way in potentiality. Whence the Philosopher says in the first book of the Physics that "things which are first manifest and certain to us are rather confused. Later, however, we know by distinguishing the principles and elements distinctly." 

It is manifest, moreover, that to know something in which many things are contained, without having proper knowledge of each of those things contained in it, is to know something under a certain confusion. In this way, both a universal whole (in which parts are contained in potentiality) and an integral whole can be known; for either whole can be known in a certain confusion without the parts being known distinctly. To know distinctly that which is contained in a universal whole is to have knowledge of a less common thing; just as knowing "animal" indistinctly is to know animal insofar as it is an animal. To know animal distinctly, however, is to know animal insofar as it is rational or irrational, which is to know a man or a lion. Therefore, it occurs to our intellect to know "animal" before knowing "man." And the same reasoning holds if we compare any more universal thing to a less universal thing. And because the sense goes out from potentiality to act just as the intellect does, the same order 

<column-break/>

of knowledge appears in the sense. For according to sense, we judge the more common before the less common, both according to place and according to time. According to place, as when something is seen from a distance, it is first grasped as being a body before it is grasped as being an animal; and it is first grasped as being an animal before it is grasped as being a man; and first as a man before as Socrates or Plato. According to time, however, because a child from the beginning first distinguishes a man from a non-man before he distinguishes this man from another man. And therefore children, from the beginning, call all men "fathers," and later they determine each one, as is said in the first book of the Physics. And the reason for this is manifest: because he who knows something indistinctly is still in potentiality to know the principle of distinction, just as he who knows the genus is in potentiality to know the difference. And thus it is clear that indistinct knowledge is midway between potentiality and act. 

It must therefore be said that the knowledge of singulars is prior for us than the knowledge of universals, just as sensitive knowledge is prior to intellectual knowledge. But both according to sense and according to intellect, knowledge of the more common is prior to knowledge of the less common. 

To the first, therefore, it must be said that the universal can be considered in two ways. In one way, according as the universal nature is considered together with the intention of universality. And since the intention of universality—namely, that one and the same thing has a relation to many—proceeds from the abstraction of the intellect, it is necessary that, according to this mode, the universal is posterior. Whence in the first book On the Soul <note>Aristotle, De Anima</note> it is said that "the universal animal is either nothing or it is posterior." But according to Plato, who posited subsistent universals, according to this consideration the universal would be prior, because particulars according to him do not exist except through participation in the subsistent universals which are called Ideas. 

In another way, it can be considered with respect to the nature itself, namely of "animality" or "humanity," as it is found in particulars. And thus it must be said that the order of nature is twofold. One is according to the way of generation and time, according to which way those things that are imperfect and in potentiality are prior. And in this way, the more common is prior according to nature, which appears manifestly in the generation of man and animal. For an animal is generated before a man, as is said in the book On the Generation of Animals. The other is the order of perfection or the intention of nature, just as act is simply prior according to nature than potentiality, and the perfect prior to the imperfect; and by this mode the less common is prior according to nature than the more common, such as man is prior to animal. For the intention of nature does not stop at the generation of an animal but intends to generate a man. 

To the second, it must be said that the more common universal is compared to the less common both as a whole and as a part. As a whole, indeed, insofar as in the more universal, there is contained in potentiality not only the less universal but also others; as under "animal" not only man but also horse is contained. As a part, however, insofar as the less common contains in its definition <note>original: "ratione"</note> not only the more common but also others, as "man" contains not only "animal" but also "rational." Thus, therefore, "animal" considered in itself is prior in our knowledge than "man." But "man" is prior in our knowledge than the fact that "animal" is a part of his definition. 

To the third, it must be said that any part can be known in two ways. In one way, absolutely according to what it is in itself, and thus nothing prevents knowing the parts before the whole, as stones before a house. In another way, according as they are parts of this whole, and thus it is necessary that we know the whole before the parts. For we first know the house with a certain confused knowledge before we distinguish its individual parts. Thus, therefore, it must be said that the defining terms considered absolutely are known before the thing defined; otherwise the thing defined would not be made known through them. <margin>Snare prepared for the tiger.</margin> animal. Under the compulsion of necessity, an art was finally invented by which he might pay the penalty for so much blood. Having scouted the narrow passes of the paths by which it was accustomed to come out at night from the hiding places of its caves for prey, the way was cut. Having dug a pit and covered it with hurdles and the excavated earth, dispersing the excess <margin>Something about the tiger.</margin> soil, they laid the trap. Coming along incautiously—it was indeed a male tiger—it fell into the pit and became impaled on sharp stakes fixed in the bottom of the ditch. With its roaring it deafened the whole neighborhood, and the mountains echoed with that shrieking. It was killed by great stones thrown down from the edges of the pit onto it while it was fixed upon the stakes. It broke into a thousand splinters and a thousand pieces the spears aimed straight at it and those hurled from above with its right paw. Even half-dead and bloodless, it filled those watching with fear; what might it have done if free and unharmed? A certain Juan Ledesma of Seville, a friend and companion in the labors of Vasco, confessed that he had eaten of that tiger. He reported to me that it was in no way inferior to beef. When asked why they call it a tiger—those who have never seen a tiger—they answer that they judge it to be a tiger by its spots, its ferocity, its agility, and other signs given by authors. Since many of them claim to have seen both leopards and spotted panthers, they follow the tracks of that killed male tiger toward the mountains and go to the communal cave, its dwelling place.

While the mother was absent, they carried off two cubs still in need of their mother's teats. Changing their plan, so that they might later send them to Spain when they had grown larger, they carefully placed iron chains around their necks and carried the little ones back to the maternal cave to be suckled. Returning to the cave a few days later, they found the cave empty with the chains in no way moved from their place. They believe they were torn to pieces by the mother in her rage and carried away so that no one might enjoy them. For they assert that they could by no means have been freed from the chains while alive. The skin of the killed tiger, stuffed with dry herbs and straw, was sent to Hispaniola to the Admiral <note>likely Diego Columbus</note> and the leading men from whom these new lands expect laws and assistance. Both those who suffered hardships from the tiger and those who handled its skin related these things to me; we accept what they give. We must return to Pacra, from whom we departed. Having entered the deserted <term>boios</term> <gloss>houses</gloss> of Pacra, Vasco strove to draw Pacra to him. Through messengers, he indicated the same things to Pacra <margin>Pacra returns.</margin> which we mentioned were indicated to the others. For a long time Pacra refused. Threats were added to his refusal. He finally came accompanied by three petty kings. Vasco writes that Pacra was so deformed, filthy, and foul that he never confessed to having seen anything more shameful. He says nature granted him <margin>The nature of Pacra; he is considered a monster.</margin> only human form; for the rest, he was a wild, monstrous, brute animal. He says his morals were equal to his habits and features. He was abusing the daughters of four neighboring petty kings, whom he had seized by force, with detestable lust. Many things concerning the obscene morals of Pacra and injuries of another kind were boasted by the neighboring petty kings in the presence of Vasco as if before a praetorian judge or indeed a vengeful Hercules, demanding that punishment be taken upon Pacra. He cast that immense beast <margin>What was done against the criminals.</margin> along with the three petty kings themselves who obeyed Pacra's command and were suffering from the same vices into the jaws of war dogs, and he ordered their mangled corpses to be burned. Wonderful things are reported concerning the dogs with which they enter battles. They rush headlong at armed natives no differently than at fleeing stags or wild boars if they are pointed out with a finger. It happened sometimes that there was no need for swords or arrows or other weapons to rout the opposing enemies; for once the signal was given and the dogs were released preceding the column, the natives, terrified by the grim appearance and unusual barking of the Molossian dogs <margin>Marvels concerning the dogs.</margin>, hesitated and, stunned by the prodigious invention, abandoned their battle lines and orders. It happens differently, however, when hands are joined in combat with the people of Cartagena and the Caribs; for they are fiercer and more apt at waging wars. They aim poisoned arrows at the rushing dogs faster than a lightning strike and kill many. The inhabitants of these mountains, however, do not wage war with arrows; they act against enemies only with <term>maccanae</term> <margin>With what weapons they wage war.</margin>, that is, broad, oblong wooden swords, and missiles and fire-hardened spears. Where his servants collected gold could never be extorted from the living Pacra by any enticements, threats, or tortures. When asked from where he had it—for they had obtained thirty pounds of gold <margin>30 pounds of gold from Pacra</margin> from his treasury—he answered that the servants who collected gold from those mountains in his parents' time and his own were dead. He had had no concern since he passed puberty for seeking gold. He could never be pulled from this resolve. From these things, conclude that it is necessary to proceed according to my prescription, and not at all according to yours. Here it is necessary that you follow me, not I you. And although you may still thunder many things against me: my Monarchy shall nevertheless stand, while yours goes to ruin. I do not write at such length about Alchemy in vain, but I do so with this intent and end: that from these things you may nearly and solidly learn what lies hidden in it, and how it ought to be understood. Nor should you be offended by this: that neither gold nor silver comes forth from it. Rather, this is what must be carefully ensured: that through it <term>arcana</term> <gloss>secret healing powers</gloss> are uncovered, and the seductions of the <term>seplasiarii</term> <gloss>perfumers or petty druggists</gloss> are exposed. By these, the unrefined common people are deceived, while these men serve them for one florin that which they would not redeem for a single penny. Such are their precious secrets.

<margin>Poison even in the best things.</margin> Who is there who would dare to deny that poison lies hidden and exists even in the best things? All are compelled to admit it. Therefore, if this is true, I now ask of you: should the poison not be separated from the good and the useful? And the good taken, the evil left behind? Indeed, it must be so. If, therefore, it is necessary: I ask you to tell me, how is it separated in your shops? For with you, all things remain mixed together. But so that you may protect your simplicity, if you are convicted into admitting that poison lies hidden there, and are asked where it finally goes: then you bring forth I know not what concerning "corrections," which supposedly drive out and take away the poison. <margin>The "correction" of the Physicians is examined.</margin> Just as they say Quince corrects Scammony, and then <term>Diagridium</term> <gloss>prepared scammony juice</gloss>. But what kind of correction is this? Does the poison not remain afterward just as it was at first? And yet you meanwhile boast that you have corrected it, so much so that the poison no longer harms. But where has it escaped to? <margin>Diagridion.</margin> It remains in the Diagridium. Try it, if you are wise: exceed the measure, and you will see where the poison is. For you will know it quite quickly. Thus you also correct <term>Turbith</term> <gloss>a purgative root</gloss>, and call it "Diaturbith." Such are your corrections, which would suit peasants, and should be given to pack-horses. Make a trial by exceeding the measure and increasing the dose: you shall see whether you will not feel the poison. <margin>What "to correct" means to Physicians.</margin> *To correct is to take what is already corrected.* He who is malicious and has sinned: if he is punished, the correction extends no further than the will of him who was punished lasts. Such are these corrections as well; the power lies with the substances themselves, not with you. Now, in this case, a Physician should consider nothing more than that the poison be removed. This must be done through separation: as, for example, a serpent is poisonous, and yet it is adopted for food. If you remove the poison from it, you may eat with no harm. The same must be understood equally concerning all other things: that there is a need for a similar separation. Until that is done, you cannot be secure in your operation; unless by chance it happens that nature supplies your deficiencies, or a greater kindness of the heavens favors you. For in your art, no protection remains.

Now then, at last, if that true foundation is required which takes away the poison, let us see how Alchemy provides it. For this must be done in such a way that, if <term>Mars</term> <gloss>Iron or the martial quality</gloss> is in the <term>Sol</term> <gloss>Gold or the solar quality</gloss>, Mars is removed; and if <term>Saturn</term> <gloss>Lead</gloss> is found in <term>Venus</term> <gloss>Copper</gloss>, it is separated from her. For as many ascendants and impressions as there are in the things of nature, so many bodies exist in them. Those bodies which are contrary, it is entirely necessary that some of them be removed and taken away, so that in this way all contrariety is abolished, and the evil is taken from the good which you seek. <margin>Fire perfects all things.</margin> As gold is useful for nothing unless it is first cast into the fire: so much less useful is a Medicine which does not pass through the fire. For it is necessary for all things to pass through the fire into a second generation, which must benefit and help man. And should this not rightly be considered the honest foundation of any Physician? For a Physician ought to apply not poisons, but <term>arcana</term> <gloss>secrets</gloss>. <margin>The shops are rebuked.</margin> However, all those preparations of the shops, as many as they are, do not contribute even a tiny letter to this doctrine. Instead, they are occupied simply in "correcting." It is as if a dog farted in a room, and that stench were lulled either by lozenges and incense, or by juniper wood: I ask you, does the stench not remain in the room afterward just as before? And though it may not be perceived by the sense of smell: is it therefore lawful for anyone to say the stench is separated and no longer remains? Indeed, it is present, but "corrected" by the fumigation. Thus the fumigation and the foul air enter the nostrils together. Such also are the corrections of the Pharmacists, who blunt an <term>Aleopaticum</term> <gloss>bitter aloe-based medicine</gloss> with sugar, so that it may thus inflict no harm. Thus sugar and honey are their entire <term>magistery</term> <gloss>mastery of the art</gloss>. Thus they even correct Gentian with <term>theriac</term> <gloss>a complex herbal jam</gloss>. Are these not the works of asinine ignorance? Yet they boast and sell themselves as the Physicians of princes. But who is so stupid as not to smell immediately that these things are worthless? What else can they boast about their remedies, I ask, except to say: *This Electuary is sweet, made of spices, sugar...*

<summary>Paracelsus argues that true medicine requires the alchemical separation of poisons from healing agents through fire, rather than the cosmetic "corrections" used by pharmacists. He compares standard pharmaceutical masking techniques, like adding sugar to bitter drugs, to using incense to hide a foul smell without actually removing the source.</summary>

But if the power of a greater natural heat should approach that quicksilver before it has been formed into its final state, namely into the form of silver, so that it is reduced into the pure and red sulfur of nature, then gold is made from it more quickly than silver, and it remains in that state perpetually, as the end toward which nature tends by its labor.

Quicksilver, which we have just mentioned, is the mother of all metals because of its coldness and humidity; and if it be pure and separated from all superfluity, then no further thickness can be mixed with it, so that it might be driven back again into some imperfect metal. For nature does not work backward, nor is it a matter that looks toward any impure form, such as imperfect metals are. But sulfur is the father of all metals because of its heat and dryness. According to this difference, let it be observed that quicksilver is described in the following chapter.

## CHAPTER II.

There is therefore in all metals a true <term>Mercury</term> <gloss>quicksilver</gloss> and a right <term>sulfur</term>, equally in imperfect as well as in perfect metals; only it has been made contaminated and impure in the imperfect metals, which are those alone that lack perfect maturation. And for these same reasons they can be reduced to gold and silver, that is, so that the impurity with which they had been defiled may be separated from the golden or silver nature that is within them, and the form of gold or silver may be introduced into them. For they were snatched away from nature for this reason: because they were removed and dug out from the natural passages, mines, and veins of the earth; therefore they can no longer have any operation within themselves, as if they were still hiding under the earth. Nevertheless, as much as is within them, they desire to be perfected.
